sections.markdown:
## C — Getting ready to drive: pre-drive checks, seat and mirror setup, belts, starting the engine, transmissions, steering methods, backing and stopping, carbon monoxide, and phone and video device laws
Knowledge domain: how a new Tennessee driver prepares the car and body before moving — what to check outside and inside, how to set the seat, head restraint and three mirrors, how to start automatic and manual cars, where the hands go and how to steer, back, pull away and stop, how to avoid carbon monoxide, and what the hands-free phone and in-car video rules forbid.

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Sections B and C of the manual are the study material for both the learner permit test and the driver license test. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
The sample questions at the end of each chapter come from the real test, but the real test can draw on many other questions, so they are a review aid rather than the full question set. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
The manual by itself cannot teach you to drive; driving skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
The online practice tests are grouped by topic, and the Guidelines for Driving practice test matches Chapters B-1 and B-2 of the manual. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A02
Before getting in, walk around the vehicle and look for small children, pets or anything else in the way. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A02
The outside check also covers the windows, lights, body damage, tire condition and any sign of fluid leaking. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A02
After getting in, put the key in the ignition, lock the doors and learn where every switch, gauge and pedal is and what it does. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A02
You should know where the horn, turn signals, four-way flashers, headlight and dimmer switch, wiper and washer controls, parking brake and release, climate and defroster controls and gearshift are even before you need them. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A02
Never drive with the seat reclined or partly reclined, because it cuts your view and slows your reaction in an emergency. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A02
Set the seat so the pedals are easy to reach and your foot can glide from accelerator to brake while your heel stays on the floor. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A02
Keep your body roughly 10 to 12 inches from the steering wheel whether or not the car has an air bag, so a deploying air bag strikes your chest instead of your chin or face. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A02
The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A02
Raise the head restraint until it is level with the back of your head, because it is there to prevent whiplash when you are struck from behind. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A02
Adjust all three rearview mirrors only after the seat is set, and always before you start driving, aiming for the widest view and the smallest blind spots. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A02
Set the inside mirror to frame the rear window, turned so that only the edge of the right rear window post shows. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A02
For the left mirror, rest your head against the driver's window and set the mirror until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A02
For the right mirror, hold your head just above the center console and set it until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A02
To check the mirrors, let a car pass on your left: as it leaves the inside mirror, its front bumper should appear in the left outside mirror. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A02
Even perfectly adjusted mirrors leave some blind spots, so always turn your head to check before turning or changing lanes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A03
Wear the lap belt snug across your hips and the shoulder belt snug across your shoulder, and make sure every passenger is belted or in a child restraint before you drive. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A03
To start most cars, keep your foot on the brake with an automatic in PARK or a manual in NEUTRAL; a manual car needs the parking brake set and the clutch pressed before it will start. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A03
With the key turned to on, check the dashboard lights and gauges, such as the antilock brake, air bag and fuel indicators, for warnings. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A03
Use low-beam headlights especially at night or in bad weather; even in normal daylight, headlights make a vehicle visible from twice as far away. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A03
In an automatic car, R is reverse and D is drive, and some newer cars add an O overdrive setting meant for interstates with little stop-and-go traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A03
The lower gears marked L, 2 or 1 are for special cases such as steep mountain descents, slow driving on ice or slippery roads, and slowing down if the brakes fail. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A03
With a manual transmission, push the clutch all the way down when starting, when shifting and once your speed falls below 10 mph while stopping. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A03
Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A03
In a car with a steering wheel interlock, never turn the ignition to lock while moving, because the wheel will lock and you will lose control. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A03
Keep both hands on the wheel with a relaxed but firm grip, and do not prop your elbow on the door or hang your arm out the window. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A03
You steer with your eyes as well as your hands: look where you want to go, and let your side vision help hold your lane position. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A03
Picture the wheel as a clock and put your left hand at 9 o'clock and your right at 3 o'clock, a position that helps avoid air bag injuries. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A03
Coming out of a turn, reverse the hand movements instead of letting the wheel slide through your fingers; this counter-steering also helps in skids and on snow and ice. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A03
Crossing your wrists during a turn is fine, but crossing your arms is not, because clothing or jewelry can snag and an air bag would injure you more. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A04
The push-pull method is the recommended way to steer because it slows the turn and keeps both hands on the wheel the whole time. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A04
Hand-over-hand steering turns the wheel faster but crosses the hands at the top and sometimes leaves only one hand on the wheel, so keep your speed down when using it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A04
New drivers backing up most often go too fast, steer too much or turn the wheel the wrong way. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A04
To back up, hold the wheel at 12 o'clock with your left hand, put your right arm over the seat back and look through the rear window, turning the wheel toward the side you want to move to. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A04
When pulling away, look at least one block ahead and steer toward a reference point. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A04
Tennessee reports rear-end collisions as the most common type of crash each year, which is why smooth, planned stops matter. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A04
At a stop sign or signal, stop before the crosswalk or marked stop line; if there is neither, stop where you can see traffic on the cross road before entering the intersection. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F41 | anchor: A04
When parking at a curb, pull within 18 inches of it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F42 | anchor: A04
Carbon monoxide from the engine can kill and cannot be tasted, smelled or seen; it tends to leak while the heater runs, when the exhaust system is faulty, or from other cars' fumes in heavy traffic. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec05-F43 | anchor: A05
Never run the engine in a closed garage, and never use the heater or air conditioner in a parked car with the windows shut. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec05-F44 | anchor: A05
Under the Hands Free Tennessee law, a driver may not hold a phone or mobile device with any part of the body or write, send or read any text-based message. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec05-F45 | anchor: A05
Since January 1, 2018, drivers aged 18 or older commit an offense by using a hand-held phone while moving through a marked school zone with its warning flashers on, unless the phone is in hands-free mode. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec05-F46 | anchor: A05
A video screen able to show television or video may not be installed where the driver can see it while the car is moving, though navigation, vehicle information and camera displays are allowed. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0044]

Misconceptions: a deploying air bag is safest when you sit back far enough for it to hit the chest, not closer; crossing wrists is allowed while crossing arms is not; lower automatic gears are for special situations, not everyday driving; properly set mirrors still leave blind spots; the hands-free rule bans holding the phone at all, not only texting.
Mnemonics: nine and three for the hands; ten to twelve inches from the wheel; seat first, then mirrors; look where you want to go.
Glossary: counter-steering means reversing your hand movements to straighten out after a turn; riding the clutch means resting a foot on the clutch pedal when not shifting; steering wheel interlock means a lock that freezes the wheel when the ignition is turned to lock; push-pull means the steering method where each hand stays on its own side of the wheel.
Dynamic facts: phone and texting penalties, the hands-free law details and the practice-test website can change; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.

items.why: seat, mirror, hand-position and steering rules are tested as multiple-choice recall, which fits the standard flashcard and quiz loop; the hands-on practice belongs to supervised driving, not the app

corpus_stability.reason: The Tennessee Comprehensive Driver License Manual says its content is current as of July 1, 2022 and its back cover carries one March 2025 print authorization; nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year, but the content date is old, so freshness is held as debt rather than assumed.
